Interpretation
in-ter-pre-ta'shun
n. (the explanation of a thing obscure; the rendering of one tongue into another; rendering Hebrew pithron, Greek hermeneia and epilusis)
From the Latin interpretatio, from interpres, an agent between parties, a translator. Greek hermeneia is from Hermes, the messenger of the Greek gods — the interpreter stands between a message and its hearer and adds nothing of his own.

Biblical Definition

Interpretation in Scripture is chiefly the unlocking of what God has said, and the Bible attributes the key to God rather than to the interpreter. Joseph states the doctrine in a prison: told that two men had dreamed and there was no interpreter, he answers, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you” (Genesis 40:8). He then interprets, but the ownership has been settled first. Before Pharaoh he is blunter still: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace” (Genesis 41:16). Daniel takes the same ground, denying that the secret was revealed to him “for any wisdom that I have more than any living” (Daniel 2:30). The pattern is uniform: the men in Scripture most gifted at interpretation are the quickest to disclaim the gift as their own. In the New Testament interpretation appears as a distinct gift of the Spirit given to the assembly, “to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:10) — and Paul's whole argument in chapter 14 is that without it, tongues must be silent, because the assembly is built by what it understands. Peter adds the governing rule for Scripture itself: no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpretation (2 Peter 1:20). The Bible is not a text each man unlocks privately; it interprets itself, Scripture by Scripture.

Webster 1828 Definition

The explanation of what is obscure. Scripture assigns the key to God, not the interpreter — do not interpretations belong to God? — and forbids private interpretation of prophecy.

expand to see more

INTERPRETATION, n. [L. interpretatio.] The act of interpreting; explanation of what is unintelligible or not understood.

2. The sense given by an interpreter; exposition.

3. The power of explaining; as, to another the interpretation of tongues, 1 Cor. 12.

4. The act of translating from one language into another.

5. In a good or bad sense; as, to put a favorable interpretation on a man's conduct.

Key Scripture

Genesis 40:8 — "And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you."

Genesis 41:16 — "And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace."

Daniel 2:30 — "But as for me, this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living, but for their sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart."

1 Corinthians 12:10 — "To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:"

Modern Corruption

Every reader is made his own final authority — what the text means to me — while the church's confessions and the rule that Scripture interprets Scripture are set aside as constraints on the individual.

expand to see more

The modern instinct is that a text has as many valid meanings as it has readers, and religious speech has absorbed it wholesale: what matters is what the passage means to you. Peter forecloses it. No prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation, because the men who wrote it did not speak by the will of man but were moved by the Holy Ghost (2 Peter 1:20-21). A text authored by one Spirit has one intended sense, and the reader's task is to find it, not to furnish it. This is why the Reformers insisted that Scripture interprets Scripture, that the clear governs the obscure, and that the analogy of faith keeps a reader from building a doctrine on a single hard verse.

The principle to recover is the interpreter's emptiness. It is not in me (Genesis 41:16) is the right posture for anyone who handles the word, and it stands against two opposite failures: the man who thinks a text yields to cleverness, and the man who thinks it yields to nothing. Confessions are the church's corporate answer to the same danger — the 1689 London Baptist Confession is a subordinate standard, binding on those who receive it and always under Scripture, and its use is precisely to keep interpretation from becoming private. A reader who has never let the church's settled reading correct him has not escaped authority; he has only reduced it to one man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pithron is the interpretation of a dream, from pathar, to open. Greek hermeneia is translation or explanation; epilusis, an unloosing, is Peter's word in 2 Peter 1:20.

expand to see more

Hebrew pithron (H6623) — interpretation, chiefly of dreams; from pathar, to open or unfold.

Hebrew pesher (H6591) — interpretation; the Aramaic term used through Daniel 2 and 5.

Greek hermeneia (G2058) — interpretation, translation; the gift of 1 Corinthians 12:10.

Greek epilusis (G1955) — an unloosing, a solution; private interpretation, 2 Peter 1:20.

Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to interpret thoroughly; the Lord expounded the Scriptures on the Emmaus road.

Usage

"Of the ownership of interpretation: do not interpretations belong to God? (Genesis 40:8)."

"Of the interpreter's emptiness: it is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace (Genesis 41:16)."

"Of interpretation as a gift to the assembly: to another the interpretation of tongues (1 Corinthians 12:10)."
